title: Transitive Dependency
description: Trace employee-to-department dependencies, identify third normal form violations, detect conflicting names, and reconstruct normalized directory reports safely.

questions.question_text: For Course(CourseID, InstructorID, InstructorOffice), assume CourseID determines InstructorID and InstructorID determines InstructorOffice. Which chain shows the resulting indirect dependency?
questions.explanation: CourseID determines InstructorID, and InstructorID determines InstructorOffice, so InstructorOffice is only indirectly (transitively) dependent on CourseID.

questions.question_text: Why is InstructorOffice's dependency on CourseID called 'transitive' rather than 'direct'?
options: Because InstructorOffice is a text field
Because there is no independent business rule linking a course directly to an office — the link only exists because the course determines its instructor, and the instructor determines the office
Because CourseID is a foreign key
questions.explanation: The dependency CourseID -> InstructorOffice is only true because it passes through the intermediate attribute InstructorID; there's no direct rule connecting courses to offices.

questions.question_text: In the introductory 3NF-violating chain X→Y→Z with nonprime Z, what must be true of the intermediate determinant Y?
options: It must be a foreign key
It is not a superkey of the examined relation
questions.explanation: A non-superkey determinant of nonprime Z violates the formal3NF condition. Being merely not a candidate key is insufficient, because a proper superkey is also not minimal.

questions.question_text: Suppose a table is already in 2NF (no partial dependency) but still has the chain CourseID -> InstructorID -> InstructorOffice. Which anomaly can STILL occur?
options: An update anomaly: changing an instructor's office still requires updating every course row taught by that instructor
An insertion anomaly for enrolling new students
A deletion anomaly when dropping a single enrollment
questions.explanation: 2NF only fixes partial dependency on the key; it does not address chains among non-key attributes, so the update anomaly for InstructorOffice can persist until 3NF removes the transitive dependency.

questions.question_text: Which decomposition removes the transitive dependency CourseID -> InstructorID -> InstructorOffice?
options: Merging Course and Instructor into one wider table
Splitting out Instructor(InstructorID, InstructorName, InstructorOffice) from Course, leaving Course(CourseID, CourseName, InstructorID) with just the foreign key
Adding a unique index on InstructorOffice
Removing InstructorID from the Course table entirely
questions.explanation: Once InstructorOffice lives in its own Instructor relation keyed directly by InstructorID, it is no longer transitively reached through CourseID.

questions.question_text: Which describes the introductory problematic chain from a key through a non-superkey determinant to a nonprime attribute?
options: Any dependency involving three or more attributes
A non-key attribute Z depends on the key only indirectly, through another non-key attribute Y, rather than directly
A dependency that changes over time
Two attributes that are both foreign keys
questions.explanation: This is the nonprime teaching case of indirect dependency. General3NF classification uses the formal superkey-or-prime condition rather than banning every implied transitive chain.

questions.question_text: In the simple nonprime teaching case, which normal form removes the problematic nonkey-to-nonprime transitive dependency left after 2NF?
questions.explanation: 3NF is formally tested on every nontrivial X→A: X is a superkey or A is prime. The simplified slogan applies only with the stated nonprime assumptions.

questions.question_text: In the fully-normalized schema (Student / Course / Instructor / Enrollment), why does Course(CourseID, CourseName, InstructorID) no longer have a transitive dependency problem for InstructorName or InstructorOffice?
options: Because those attributes are deleted entirely
Because InstructorName and InstructorOffice no longer live in the Course table at all — they now depend directly on InstructorID inside the separate Instructor table
Because CourseID now directly determines InstructorOffice by rule
Because Course now has a composite key
questions.explanation: Moving InstructorName/InstructorOffice into their own Instructor relation removes the transitive chain entirely — Course only keeps the foreign key InstructorID, with no dependent attribute traveling further.

questions.question_text: Given employee_id to department_id and department_id to department_name, what follows?
options: department_id must be an employee key
questions.explanation: Transitivity permits the composed dependency.

questions.question_text: Why is department_id not a superkey of the employee relation here?
options: Several employees may share one department
The table has a primary key
questions.explanation: A superkey must uniquely identify an employee row.

questions.question_text: Where should department_name be authoritatively stored after decomposition?
questions.explanation: Department identity determines its descriptive name.

questions.question_text: What does a clean dependency audit prove?
options: The business rule holds for every future state
No examined rows show the tested conflict
questions.explanation: Observed consistency is evidence about the examined data, not a universal semantic proof.

questions.question_text: Why can COUNT(DISTINCT name) miss missing names?
options: It counts NULL as every name
questions.explanation: Missing values need a separate policy and diagnostic.

questions.question_text: What is a prime attribute?
options: An attribute belonging to at least one candidate key
questions.explanation: Prime status depends on candidate key membership.

questions.question_text: Which condition permits a nontrivial dependency under 3NF?
options: The determinant is a superkey or the dependent attribute is prime
The table has exactly two columns
questions.explanation: The formal third normal form condition uses superkeys and prime attributes.

questions.question_text: What ensures at most one department match per employee in the decomposed join?
options: Both tables share a column spelling
questions.explanation: Key uniqueness prevents a department join from multiplying rows.

questions.question_text: Does adding an employee row surrogate remove the department dependency?
options: Only when the surrogate is BIGINT
questions.explanation: A row identifier does not change which attributes determine department names.

questions.question_text: What should happen to conflicting names before a department backfill?
options: Resolve them using an approved source of truth
Delete every employee in the group
questions.explanation: Arbitrary aggregation conceals unresolved facts.

questions.question_text: What can make department_id alone insufficient to determine a historical name?
options: The model includes versioned names over time
questions.explanation: Temporal semantics may require a version or effective interval.

questions.question_text: Which join retains employees with optional missing department assignments?
questions.explanation: A left join preserves the employee side when optional matches are absent.

original_questions.question_text: What is required of the intermediate attribute Y (here, InstructorID) for X -> Y -> Z to count as a genuine transitive dependency (rather than a harmless key chain)?
options: Y must be a foreign key referencing another table
Y must NOT itself be a candidate key of the relation being examined
Y must be the same data type as Z

original_questions.question_text: Which is the best one-line definition of transitive dependency?

A non-key attribute Z depends on the key only indirectly, through another non-key attribute Y, rather than directly
A dependency that changes over time
Two attributes that are both foreign keys
original_questions.explanation: Transitive dependency specifically describes an indirect chain (X -> Y -> Z) where Z's dependency on X passes through an intermediate non-key attribute Y.

original_questions.question_text: Which normal form is defined as '2NF plus no transitive dependency on the key'?
original_questions.explanation: 3NF's definition builds directly on 2NF by additionally requiring that no non-key attribute be transitively dependent on the key.

coding_problems.title: Detect Department Name Conflicts
coding_problems.task: Return department_id for groups having more than one distinct department_name. Names are NOT NULL. Order by department_id.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE directory (employee_id INT PRIMARY KEY,department_id INT NOT NULL,department_name VARCHAR(60) NOT NULL);
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT department_id FROM directory GROUP BY department_id HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT department_name)>1 ORDER BY department_id;
coding_problems.ordering: Order rows by the key specified in the task.
edge_cases: Empty input returns no detail rows.
Include equal values on different source rows.
Verify boundary and NULL handling when the schema permits them.
hints: Determine the result grain before writing the query.
Use explicit projected columns and a final ORDER BY.
coding_problems.explanation: The solution implements the stated row selection and preserves the requested result grain; the final ordering makes comparisons deterministic.

coding_problems.title: Reconstruct the Normalized Directory
coding_problems.task: Return employee_id, employee_name, department_name for every employee. Departments are mandatory and keyed by department_id. Order by employee_id.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE departments (department_id INT PRIMARY KEY,department_name VARCHAR(60) NOT NULL); CREATE TABLE employees (employee_id INT PRIMARY KEY,employee_name VARCHAR(60) NOT NULL,department_id INT NOT NULL);

notes:
## Follow a chain of determining facts

An employee directory stores employee_id, employee_name, department_id, and department_name. Each employee has one department in this simplified model, and each department identifier has one official name. Employee identity determines department identity, which determines department name. The employee row therefore repeats a fact owned by the department. This dependency chain helps explain why a department rename requires many employee updates and why a department without employees is awkward to represent.

A functional dependency X determines Y means that any two valid rows agreeing on X must agree on Y. It is a rule about every valid state allowed by the business model. It does not merely mean that the current sample happens to contain one Y for each X. Transitivity is the inference that X determines Z when X determines Y and Y determines Z. For normalization, the troublesome case often involves a nonkey attribute determining another nonkey attribute.

## Write the dependencies before decomposing

Assume employee_id is the only candidate key in this example. The dependencies are employee_id to employee_name and department_id, and department_id to department_name. The department identifier is not a superkey of the employee relation because several employees can share it. The department name is nonprime because it is not part of a candidate key. These details explain the third normal form issue precisely.

```sql
CREATE TABLE employee_directory (
 employee_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
 employee_name VARCHAR(60) NOT NULL,
 department_id INT NOT NULL,
 department_name VARCHAR(60) NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO employee_directory VALUES
 (1,'Asha',10,'Engineering'),
 (2,'Rohan',10,'Engineering'),
 (3,'Neha',20,'Sales');
```

Employee 1 determines department 10, and department 10 determines Engineering. The same department description is stored in employees 1 and 2. If employee 2 instead says Platform, the sample violates the stated department dependency. Such a row is not evidence that functional dependency theory is wrong. It is either invalid data under the rule or a signal that the business model was stated incorrectly.

If departments can have historical names, a timeless department_id to name rule may be insufficient. A department version or effective interval can determine the applicable name. If employees can hold several simultaneous assignments, the employee to department rule also changes. Normalization starts with accurate semantics, so identify time and multiplicity before applying a memorized decomposition.

## Why the chain causes anomalies

An update anomaly occurs when a department rename is made on some employee rows but not others. A deletion anomaly occurs when removing the last employee also removes the only record of that department's official name. An insertion anomaly occurs when a new department cannot be entered until an employee is invented. Each symptom follows from making employee rows the only place to store an independently determined department fact.

Adding a surrogate row identifier does not remove the chain. Employee_id already identifies rows; the problem is which determinant owns department_name. An index on department_id may speed a search, but it does not stop two employee rows from giving the same department conflicting names. Physical access and logical dependency are different design concerns.

## Decompose around the determinant

Create departments with department_id as its key and department_name as its dependent attribute. Keep employee identity, name, and department reference in employees. A foreign key requires each employee assignment to reference a real department. The department can now exist without any employees, and a rename is represented in one authoritative row.

```sql
CREATE TABLE departments (
 department_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
 department_name VARCHAR(60) NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE employees (
 employee_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
 employee_name VARCHAR(60) NOT NULL,
 department_id INT NOT NULL,
 FOREIGN KEY (department_id) REFERENCES departments(department_id)
);
INSERT INTO departments VALUES (10,'Engineering'),(20,'Sales'),(30,'Research');
INSERT INTO employees VALUES (1,'Asha',10),(2,'Rohan',10),(3,'Neha',20);
SELECT e.employee_id,e.employee_name,d.department_name
FROM employees e
JOIN departments d ON d.department_id=e.department_id
ORDER BY e.employee_id;
```

The expected display reconstructs Asha Engineering, Rohan Engineering, and Neha Sales. Research remains present in departments even with no employees. These are reasoned outputs from the fixture, not an execution claim. The decomposition changes storage ownership while preserving the ability to query the useful combined information.

The common attribute department_id is a key of departments, so each employee matches at most one department row. This explains why the join does not multiply employee rows when the constraints hold. If department identity is not unique, a join can invent combinations and duplicate employees in the reconstructed display. Lossless reconstruction depends on the dependency and key design rather than the mere presence of a JOIN keyword.

## Preserve dependencies as enforceable contracts

In the split design, a department primary key directly enforces one stored name per department identity. The employee foreign key enforces that a referenced department exists. Those constraints have separate roles: uniqueness alone does not stop an orphan reference, and a foreign key alone does not establish the correctness of a human chosen name. Review both successful writes and denied writes when implementing the design in an authorized database environment. A successful reconstructed SELECT is useful evidence about reads, but it does not test duplicate department rejection or invalid assignment rejection.

## State the third normal form rule carefully

A relation is in third normal form when, for every nontrivial functional dependency X to A that holds, X is a superkey or A is a prime attribute. A prime attribute belongs to some candidate key. The familiar instruction to remove transitive nonkey dependencies works for many simple examples, but the formal condition handles relations with multiple candidate keys more accurately. Do not claim that every transitive inference in all schemas must be removed.

In the employee example department_id is not a superkey and department_name is not prime, so that dependency violates the condition. After decomposition, department_id is a key in departments, and employee attributes depend on employee identity in employees. This reasoning explains the result instead of relying only on the number of tables or whether a column name ends in id.

## Detect conflicting observations with SQL

A data audit can find observed department identifiers having more than one distinct name. Group the mixed data by department_id and use COUNT(DISTINCT department_name) > 1. The query is a useful diagnostic, but a clean result does not prove the dependency as a universal rule. It only establishes that the examined rows contain no detected disagreement under that comparison.

NULL requires care. COUNT(DISTINCT department_name) ignores NULL, so a nullable design can hide missing names during this audit. Decide whether missing names are invalid, whether they should be flagged separately, or whether they represent an approved state. The teaching schema uses NOT NULL so the audit has a straightforward meaning. String collation can also affect whether two spellings are considered distinct.

## Worked lab: find conflicting department names

Start with employee 1 in department 10 named Engineering and employee 2 in department 10 named Platform. Add employee 3 in department 20 named Sales. The task is to return department 10 only. The solution groups by department_id, counts distinct names, and keeps groups above one. Two employees repeating Engineering are not a conflict; two different department identifiers both called Services are also not a violation of department_id determining name.

Before backfilling departments, resolve each reported disagreement through an approved source of truth. Do not use MIN or MAX as a convenient arbitrary answer. Such an aggregation can make a migration run while destroying evidence about conflicting facts. Preserve the original identifiers and establish the correct department assignment and name first.

## Worked lab: preserve the employee display

A second task queries the decomposed tables and returns one row per employee with the department name. Join on department_id, project explicit columns, and order by employee_id. Test multiple employees in one department, two departments sharing a display name, and a department with no employees. The employee display should preserve all employees without generating a row for the empty department unless the report asks for department coverage.

If department assignment is optional, make that rule explicit and use a left join when the display must retain unassigned employees. Do not weaken a mandatory foreign key rule just to demonstrate NULL behavior. Query shape follows the actual optionality contract.

Read [Insertion Anomaly](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/insertion-anomaly) for the independent-fact lifecycle and [Simple Views](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/simple-views) for exposing a stable reconstructed display. No production schema, constraint, or migration was changed by these examples.
